title: Keep coroutine inputs alive across suspension
summary: Give suspended work an owner and ensure every borrowed object outlives its use.
objectives: Identify data retained by a suspended coroutine.
Distinguish a copied owning parameter from a borrowed reference.
Explain cleanup when a task is abandoned before completion.

blocks.text: Suspension separates the caller’s progress from the coroutine body’s progress. An argument supplied by reference remains a reference; a coroutine frame does not turn it into an owned copy of the referent. An object local to the caller can disappear before suspended work uses it. Captured this pointers, views, and references all deserve the same lifetime review.

Passing a std::string by value lets the coroutine retain an owning parameter. The copy or move into coroutine state has a cost, but that cost can be the correct price of an interface that allows the caller to continue. Passing std::string_view by value would only copy a view. Always inspect the ownership semantics of the parameter type, not just whether its declaration contains an ampersand.

blocks.caption: main.cpp — C++20

blocks.text: The temporary supplied by main can expire after the call because the coroutine’s value parameter owns its own string. The first resume prints Atlas and suspends. Then task is destroyed. Destroying the suspended frame cleans up its state without executing the remaining finished output. The wrapper has the same single-thread, suspended-frame invariant as the previous lesson.

This is abandonment of a local teaching task, not a protocol for canceling an external operation. If an event loop has retained a handle, destroying the frame while it can still resume that handle creates a lifetime bug. A real runtime must coordinate operation cancellation, unregistration, outstanding callbacks, and frame destruction.

blocks.prompt: Would changing announce to accept const std::string& preserve the temporary’s lifetime until resume?
blocks.explanation: No. The reference parameter would refer to a temporary that expires after the call expression. Initial suspension happens before the body uses it, so a later resume would access an expired object.

blocks.text: For each suspension point, list the objects needed afterward and who keeps them alive. Test early completion and abandonment as deliberately as the success path. Library task types can package these rules, but their ownership, cancellation, and exception contracts must be read. C++23 supplies std::generator for a particular synchronous generator use case; it does not retroactively make all C++20 coroutine return types standard task abstractions.
